standard_prerequisites.name: Finite directed-graph reachability and depth-first search
standard_prerequisites.statement: Reach(v) is the set of vertices accessible by directed paths, and can be found by depth-first search.
standard_prerequisites.use: Find a path bringing one pebble to an endpoint; no sparsity or matroid theorem is assumed.

core_obligations: Identify and establish conservation of pebbles plus outgoing edges for vertices and subsets.
Prove the lower bound on pebbles plus boundary edges despite layer-dependent sparsity thresholds, separating current, immediately preceding, and earlier edge layers.
For a sparse graph, use the closed union of the two endpoint reachability sets and the still-missing edge to force an available external pebble.
Show that repeated path reversals increase the pebble count at the two endpoints until the edge is accepted; combine with the invariants for both recognition directions.

proof_roadmap.step: Establish all four invariants. The nonconstant threshold is controlled by edge-processing order and the two strict parameter inequalities.
Convert the subset invariant into sparsity, and total conservation into tightness.
Under the explicitly stated sparse-graph premise, the endpoint reachability set has no outgoing edge and contains a missing edge; conservation gives a strict pebble surplus.
Iterate the reachability move to accept every edge.

difficulty_reason: The substantive obligation is a correctness proof for a layered extension of the pebble game with different sparsity deficits at different ranks. Conservation alone is insufficient: the invariant must exploit the processing order and distinguish three layer cases, then be combined with a closed reachability-set obstruction to force progress. No matroid structure, surplus-independence lemma, or correctness of an earlier pebble game is supplied as a shortcut.

compared.difference: The published item is invariance of a minimization surplus under changing maximal feasible sets. The present target is soundness and completeness of the rank-ordered pebble algorithm and its subset/reachability invariants, independent of that argument.

compared.difference: No layered-graph pebble recognition algorithm or reachable-set tightness obstruction; the new two-direction algorithm theorem is independent of this abstract flat property.
